name: Hinuq
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Stress is not a very prominent category in Hinuq. The stress properties of Hinuq words are very hard to determine. The stress is quite weak such that even native speakers have difficulties or are even unable to figure out the stress in elicitation. [...] However, one feature of stress assignment in Hinuq seems to hold for most of the words in my material: heavy syllables of the type CVC or CV: usually attract stress, e.g. dán.di 'against', i.žéy 'eye', o.čór.di.yu 'old'. [...] nouns, pronouns, and postpositions/adverbs are mostly stressed on the first syllable. [...] [if there is no] heavy syllable, stress falls mostly on the first syllable. Loans from Russian are nowadays stressed in the same way as in Russian.
new_statements.citation: Forker, Diana. 2013. A Grammar of Hinuq (Mouton Grammar Library 63). Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110303971
new_statements.locator: §2.5 Word stress, pp. 49–53 (2.5.1 Stress in roots, p. 49; 2.5.2 Stress in major parts of speech, pp. 50–51; 2.5.4 Stress in loan words, p. 53); page numbers from the Google Books TOC snippet and Borise's citation 'Forker 2013: 49'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak, hard-to-hear word stress. Heavy syllables (closed CVC or long-vowel CVː) usually attract the stress; in words without a heavy syllable stress falls mostly on the first syllable (nouns, pronouns, postpositions/adverbs mostly initial; demonstratives on the second syllable; disyllabic adjectives initial, trisyllabic adjectives second syllable; verbs by conjugation class — per Borise's summary of Forker, stem-final -i verbs initial, stem-final -e verbs second syllable). Many loans keep source-language stress (often final; Avar loans as in Avar, Russian loans as in Russian).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Forker 2013: 'Trisyllabic nouns can bear the main stress on the first syllable and a secondary stress on the last syllable' (snippet, §2.5.2, p. 50–51).
new_statements.exceptions: Some words have variable stress (-égi/-egí 'good', -éži/-eží 'big, old'); many loans stressed on the final syllable (bazár 'market', halmáy 'friend', duniyál 'world'); stress of enclitics and suffixes left for future research. Conflicting older first-hand claim: Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 330 state that word stress is absent, the language is apparently tonal (tones uninvestigated), and phrasal accent falls on the word's beginning or on a non-initial closed syllable — Borise 2018 reads this as the same heavy-syllable tendency taken as phrasal. Lomtadze 1963: 27 (per Borise) instead posits lexical stem-initial vs stem-final classes with stress mobile to the final stem syllable in oblique case forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, elicited citation forms (Forker notes speakers' difficulty in elicitation); Kibrik & Kodzasov treat the prominence as phrase-level. Forker's quote is assembled from verbatim Google Books search snippets ('[...]' marks gaps), not from an opened page; the full page needs verification against the book.
new_statements.identity_note: Hinuq is a one-village language (Genux/Hinuq village, Tsunta district, Dagestan) with no dialect division; all sources describe the same variety (hinu1240). Older Soviet-era works (Lomtadze 1963; Imnaišvili 1963; Kibrik & Kodzasov's part-heading) treat it as the 'Hinukh dialect of Dido (Tsez)', but the object is the same language.

sources.citation: Borise, Lena. 2018. Word stress in the languages of the Caucasus (lingbuzz/004203 ms.; published 2021 in M. Polinsky (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Languages of the Caucasus, OUP), Hinuq paragraph, ms. pp. 21–22
sources.note: Secondary survey: 'Hinuq stress is acoustically weak (Lomtadze 1963: 34; Forker 2013: 49), and its distribution is poorly understood. Forker (2013: 49) notes a tendency for stress to target heavy (CVC or CVː) syllables. So do Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 330), though they take the phenomenon in question to be phrasal stress.' Reports Lomtadze 1963: 27 as stem-initial vs stem-final lexical classes (χému 'stone' vs barú 'wife'), plural -be attracting stress in the latter, final stem syllable stressed in oblique case forms, postpositions attracting stress; verbs: stem-final -i → first syllable, stem…

sources.citation: Kibrik, A. E. & S. V. Kodzasov. 1990. Sopostavitel'noe izučenie dagestanskix jazykov. Imja. Fonetika. Moscow: Izd-vo MGU. Part Fonetika, §8 Ginuxskij jazyk, 'Slog i prosodija', p. 330
sources.note: 'Гинухский язык, очевидно, является тональным, однако тоны не были исследованы. Словесное ударение отсутствует. Фразовый акцент ставится либо на начало выделяемого слова, либо на его неначальный закрытый слог.' = apparently tonal (tones uninvestigated); no word stress; phrasal accent on the word's beginning or on a non-initial closed syllable.
Silent on stress; bibliographies list Forker 2013, Lomtadze 1963, Bokarev 1959, Xalilov & Isakov 2005 dictionary.
